auxiliary_passages.statement_original: We use regular letters, bold regular letters and bold capital letters to denote scalars, vectors and matrices respectively. For any positive integer $n$, we denote $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ by $[n]$. For any two sets $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$, let $\mathcal A\setminus\mathcal B:=\mathcal A\cap\mathcal B^c$. For any vector $\mathbf a$ and matrix $\mathbf A$, we use $\mathbf a^\top$ and $\mathbf A^\top$ to denote the transpose of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf A$ respectively. Given $\mathcal B=\{i_1,\ldots,i_{|\mathcal B|}\}\subset[p]$, we use $\mathbf X_{\mathcal B}$ to denote the submatrix of $\mathbf X$ with columns indexed in $\mathcal B$ and $\beta_{\mathcal B}$ to denote $(\beta_{i_1},\ldots,\beta_{i_{|\mathcal B|}})^\top$. Given any $a,b\in\mathbb R$, we say $a\lesssim b$ if there exists a universal constant $C>0$ such that $a\leq Cb$; we say $a\gtrsim b$ if there exists a universal constant $c>0$ such that $a\geq cb$; we say $a\asymp b$ if $a\lesssim b$ and $a\gtrsim b$. For any event $\mathcal A$, we use $I(\mathcal A)$ to denote the indicator function associated with $\mathcal A$, i.e., $I(\mathcal A)=1$ if $\mathcal A$ occurs, and $I(\mathcal A)=0$ otherwise.
auxiliary_passages.resolution_note: Set operations, subvectors, indicator-based sparsity and transpose notation are source conventions. Bold vector typography is normalized in extracted math; mathematical dimensions are retained.

auxiliary_passages.statement_original: Throughout this section, we write the $n\times p$ design matrix $\mathbf X=(\mathbf X_1,\ldots,\mathbf X_p)$ and the $n\times q$ matrix $\mathbf Z=(\mathbf Z_1,\ldots,\mathbf Z_q)$, where $\mathbf X_j$ and $\mathbf Z_k$ are the $j$th and $k$th columns of $\mathbf X$ and $\mathbf Z$, respectively.
auxiliary_passages.resolution_note: Matrix dimensions are available to deterministic grouping sensitivity and oracle calculations without treating the Gaussian error law as a prerequisite of those definitions.

auxiliary_passages.statement_original: Denote the solution of the $L_0$-Fusion problem (2.1) by $\widehat\theta^{\mathrm g}=(\widehat\beta^{\mathrm g\top},\widehat\alpha^{\mathrm g\top})^\top$. Recall that $K_0=|\mathbb G(\beta^*)|$ and further define $s_0=\|\beta^*\|_0$.
auxiliary_passages.resolution_note: K0 counts distinct nonzero coefficient values and s0 counts nonzero coordinates; they are not interchangeable.

auxiliary_passages.statement_original: Algorithm 2 is essentially a projected gradient descent algorithm: In each iteration, we perform a gradient descent step followed by projection onto $\mathcal H_{K,s}$. To obtain an element in $\mathcal H_{K,s}(\mathbf c)$ for any $\mathbf c\in\mathbb R^{p+q}$, we can exploit the subroutine Algorithm 3 in Appendix A.1, which is a generalization of the segment neighborhood method (Auger and Lawrence, 1989) with sparsity constraint.
auxiliary_passages.resolution_note: The main text defines the projection mathematically by its argmin. The appendix subroutine is referenced but is not expanded or used as an additional theorem prerequisite.

standard_ambient_resolution: The parameter theta concatenates beta in R^p and nuisance alpha in R^q. The existence of a gamma vector supplies at most K distinct nonzero beta values; repeated or zero gamma entries are not ruled out by the feasible-set definition.
The grouping operator excludes zero coefficients, while its index operator includes the zero class when evaluated at r=0. Group counts and support sizes have distinct meanings.

The distance of Definition 2.1 uses injections from the smaller nonzero grouping into the larger one. Its asymmetric definition is valid for the candidate-vs-truth comparison in c_min because the feasible class bounds candidate group count by the true count.

The statistical probability statements use the regression model and iid observation convention. The deterministic grouping sensitivity, parameter class and projection definitions do not themselves require Gaussian sampling.

Theorem 2.5 defines r(X,Z,K0,s0) inside its own statement. No extra API is invented for that local binder. Its estimator infimum ranges over arbitrary estimators of the grouping under the stated sampling model.

Theorem 3.2 uses a general convex, lower-bounded objective with Lipschitz gradient as specified in Section 3.2. It does not require the squared-error objective, Gaussian errors, a true grouping, or the statistical parameter subclasses.
The squared Euclidean projection is set-valued. Algorithm 2 selects an element at each step; the theorem does not specify a unique projection or a particular implementation.
Theorem 3.2 supplies the limiting real constant c with g(theta_m) decreasing to c. It is not defined as the global minimum or the lower-bound constant C2.

unresolved_source_conventions.text: The source specifies a scalar Gaussian error law and iid observations but does not explicitly state independence of the error from the covariates in this passage. No conditional-error or design assumption is inserted.

The set-builder lists gamma in R^K without writing an existential quantifier. The source constraint is retained; the auxiliary gamma is understood as a feasibility witness, without requiring K distinct occupied groups.

The minima and least-squares solutions are printed without attainment or uniqueness assumptions. The group-equality oracle constraint and the subsequent unrestricted collapsed-design regression need not define the same set if fitted groups merge or vanish. Both source formulations are retained without adding design-rank or nonzero-coefficient conditions.

The balanced subclass uses group labels indexed by K0 although Theta(K0,s0) is an upper-bound class; no exact-group-count restriction is inserted. The ratio r can have a zero or undefined denominator, and the displayed parameter range permits floor((K0+3)/4)*p=1, making the logarithmic denominator zero. No extra positivity, cardinality or empty-class convention is supplied.

The Lipschitz-gradient condition is stated for points in Theta(K,s), but Algorithm 2 initializes theta1 anywhere in R^(p+q). The source does not explicitly require a feasible initialization; no such requirement is added.

The algorithm prints a stopping tolerance, while Theorem 3.2 concerns its infinite update sequence and every positive integer M. The source does not state an extension after termination. The finite algorithm and infinite-sequence theorem are preserved separately.

excluded_proof_dependencies: The sure-screening event and CoSaMP Algorithm 1 pertain to a corollary or applications, not these three Theorems. The MIO formulation, first-order stationary-point definition and preceding convergence propositions are not additional premises of Theorem 3.2.

The restricted-eigenvalue discussion after Theorem 2.5 is explicitly conjectural or illustrative and is not inserted into the theorem hypotheses. Appendix-only proofs and Algorithm 3 are not extracted.
